topic.title: Natural selection, evolution, extinction and selective breeding
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: A B2 Higher question of 4 to 7 marks in every recent summer paper. The Summer 2024 report calls natural selection a topic candidates find difficult: the marks go to answers that keep to the chain (variation, the others die, the resistant survive and reproduce, the gene is passed on) and answer about the population the question names.
mustMemorise: Variation in the phenotypes of a population comes first
Competition for resources: the best adapted are more likely to survive
The survivors reproduce, and their offspring inherit their genes
Antibiotic resistance is natural selection: the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria
Evolution: a continuing process of natural selection, gradual change over time, may form a new species
Extinction: a species fails to adapt to a change in its environment
Selective breeding: humans select for a desirable characteristic and breed, over many generations
notOnThisSpec: Fossils and the other evidence for evolution
The history of Darwin and Wallace and how the theory was received
How new species form in detail, such as isolation
Inbreeding and its problems in selective breeding

mustBeAbleTo: Explain resistance in a population as natural selection, one mark a link: variation, the others die, the resistant survive and reproduce, they pass on the gene
Put the stages of natural selection in order, and sort examples into natural selection and selective breeding
Read a population diagram or a dish of bacteria: what survives, how many, what percentage
Explain why the middle of a range is commonest, and predict how the curve moves when the environment changes
Describe evolution as a continuing process of natural selection that may form new species (Higher Tier), and explain extinction as a failure to adapt
Describe selective breeding over many generations, choose parents from data and name what each one brings
Calculate a percentage, and a percentage increase, from counts or yields
sheet.howExamined: One question of 4 to 7 marks on the B2 Higher paper in every recent summer: 2021 Q9 (sort, order, name evolution and extinction), 2022 Q9 (a range of neck lengths and a curve to continue), 2023 Q5 (choose parent plants and explain; other characteristics to select), 2024 Q9 (a four-mark chain, then the advantage to the other population) and 2025 Q7(a) (a dish of bacteria: two changes, then complete stage C). Evolution forming new species is Higher Tier; extinction and selective breeding are Foundation.
traps: Writing about immunity and antibodies to explain a resistant population, instead of the passing on of the resistance gene (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q9)
Giving the effect on the other species when the advantage to the named population is asked for (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q9)
Drawing original bacteria still present after the antibiotic, where only resistant ones remain (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q7)
Choosing the right parents but explaining carelessly, without naming what each one brings (Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q5)
Saying individuals change or adapt to survive: the difference is already there, and the population changes because of who survives and breeds

workedExamples.stem: Head lice used to be killed by a particular shampoo. Now most head lice in one town are resistant to it. Use what you know about natural selection to explain how this happened. [4]

steps.working: Some lice had a mutation that made them resistant to the shampoo.
steps.decision: Start with variation, before the shampoo was ever used. This line stops the answer from saying the lice changed.

options: Selection can only keep a difference that is already there
Every louse becomes a little resistant
whyMenu.explain: The shampoo does not create resistance; it removes the lice without it. So the resistant ones must have been there first.

steps.working: The shampoo killed the lice that were not resistant.
steps.decision: Say what happens to the others. That is the selection.

steps.working: The resistant lice survived and reproduced.
steps.decision: Survived and reproduced, together: surviving alone changes nothing in the next generation.

steps.working: They passed the resistance gene on to their offspring.
steps.decision: The link the Summer 2024 report found missing. End on the gene being passed on.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Some lice had a mutation that made them resistant; the shampoo killed the others; the resistant lice survived and reproduced, and passed the resistance gene on to their offspring.

accepted: the resistant mosquitoes passed the resistance gene on to their offspring

workedExamples.stem: A grower has four pepper plants. Plant P: many small peppers. Plant Q: few large peppers. Plant R: few small peppers, resists disease. Plant S: few small peppers. She wants plants with large peppers that resist disease. Give the letters of the two plants she should breed together, and explain your answer. [2]

steps.working: Large peppers: only Q has them.
steps.decision: Take the characteristics one at a time and find the plant that has each.
The second characteristic, found the same way.
Their offspring can inherit both characteristics.

steps.working: Q has large peppers and R resists disease.
steps.decision: The explanation names what each plant brings. The Summer 2023 report found the right letters with a careless explanation.

options: The mark is for naming each plant's characteristic
Saying they are the best plants is enough
The letters alone earn both marks
whyMenu.explain: An examiner looks for the characteristic each chosen plant brings; 'the best' names nothing.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Q and R: Q has large peppers and R resists disease.

twin.stem: Use the same four pepper plants. The grower now wants plants that give many peppers and resist disease. Which two plants should she breed together?

options.feedback: P gives many peppers and R resists disease.
P gives many peppers, but Q does not resist disease. R does.
R resists disease, but Q gives few peppers. P gives many.
R resists disease, but S gives few peppers. P gives many.

workedExamples.stem: After 5 generations of selective breeding, the mean milk yield of a herd rose from 25.0 to 30.0 litres per cow per day. Calculate the percentage increase. [2]

steps.decision: A percentage increase starts from the size of the change.
Divide by the value you started from, not the value you finished at.

options: An increase is measured against where it started
The larger number always goes on the bottom
whyMenu.explain: A percentage increase compares the rise with the starting value.

steps.decision: Five generations for a fifth more milk: each generation moved the herd a little.

twin.stem: Selective breeding raised the mean wool yield of a flock of sheep from 3.2 kg to 4.0 kg per sheep. Calculate the percentage increase. [2]

items.stem: Before the lesson, three things from earlier topics; nobody expects you to know this lesson yet. What is a mutation?

options.text: a random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene
options.feedback: A random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene. It is where new variation comes from.

options.text: a change an organism makes so that it survives
options.feedback: Mutations are random. An organism cannot choose one.
That is an infection, not a mutation.

options.text: an injury such as a scar
options.feedback: A scar is caused by the environment and is not in the genes.

items.stem: How are characteristics passed from parents to their offspring?

options.text: in the genes carried by the gametes
options.feedback: Through the genes in the gametes: sperm and egg, or pollen and ovule.

options.text: by the offspring copying its parents
options.feedback: Behaviour can be learned, but an inherited characteristic comes from genes.

options.text: through the blood the offspring shares with its mother
options.feedback: Characteristics are inherited through genes, not blood.
Offspring of sexual reproduction inherit genes from both parents.

options.text: it kills bacteria or stops them growing
options.feedback: It kills bacteria or slows their growth. It does nothing to viruses.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.

options.text: it makes the body produce antibodies
options.feedback: That is what a vaccine does. An antibiotic is a chemical that acts on bacteria.
An antibiotic does not create resistance; it kills the bacteria that lack it.

items.stem: What must there be in a population before natural selection can act?

options.feedback: Variation. Selection can only keep a characteristic that some individuals already have.
Individuals do not change to fit the environment; some are different to begin with.
The population can stay the same size while its proportions change.
An antibiotic is one thing that can do the selecting. It is not needed for natural selection.

items.stem: An antibiotic is added to a dish of resistant and non-resistant bacteria. Which bacteria are there a day later?

options.feedback: Resistant only: the antibiotic kills the others, and the resistant ones keep dividing.

options.text: both kinds, in the same proportions
options.feedback: The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria. The Summer 2025 report found many drawings still showing them.
That is the wrong way round: the resistant ones are the survivors.
The resistant bacteria are not killed. They survive and divide.

items.stem: Why does the proportion of resistant bacteria rise over many generations?

options.text: the resistant ones survive, reproduce and pass on the gene for resistance
options.feedback: Survive, reproduce, pass on the gene: that is the whole chain.

options.text: the bacteria change to become resistant when they meet the antibiotic
options.feedback: No bacterium changes to survive. Some were resistant already.

options.text: the bacteria make antibodies against the antibiotic
options.feedback: Bacteria do not make antibodies. The Summer 2024 report found this confusion.
Surviving is not enough. They must reproduce and pass on the gene.

options.text: a continuing process of natural selection that causes gradual change over time
options.feedback: A continuing process of natural selection, causing gradual change, which can form new species.

options.text: a sudden change in one individual
options.feedback: Evolution happens to populations, gradually, over many generations.

options.text: the breeding of animals by humans
options.feedback: That is selective breeding.

options.text: the death of every member of a species
options.feedback: That is extinction.

items.stem: A species becomes extinct after its environment changes. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: none of its individuals had characteristics suited to the new conditions
options.feedback: With no suitable variation, none survived to reproduce.

options.text: its individuals chose not to adapt
options.feedback: Adapting is not a choice. Selection can only work on variation that is already there.
Producing many offspring is normal; it is what causes competition.
More variation makes it more likely that some individuals survive, not less.

items.stem: In selective breeding, what decides which individuals breed?
items.skill: Tell selective breeding from natural selection

options.text: humans, choosing those with a desirable characteristic
options.feedback: Humans choose. Everything else in the chain is the same as natural selection.
That is natural selection.
The breeder chooses on purpose.
The breeder makes the choice, generation after generation.

items.stem: Why does selective breeding take many generations?

options.text: each round makes the characteristic a little more common, so it is repeated until all the offspring show it
options.feedback: Each generation shifts the proportion a little; only repeated selection makes it universal.

options.text: the animals need time to learn the characteristic
options.feedback: The characteristic is inherited, not learned.

options.text: the breeder has to make the mutations first
options.feedback: The breeder selects from variation that is already there.
One round changes the proportion only a little.

context.setting: Naming the two processes by who does the choosing

hints: People choose which ones breed.
parts.stem: Name the process in which humans choose which plants or animals breed, so that a characteristic they want becomes common.

any: selective breeding
selectively breeding
selectively bred
selective breed
artificial selection

scheme.for: selective breeding

parts.workedSolution: Selective breeding.

hints: Nobody chooses: the environment decides.
parts.stem: Name the process in which the individuals best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and breed.

any: natural selection
naturally selected
natural selecting
survival of the fittest

scheme.for: natural selection
scheme.examinerNote: Natural selection is the name to learn; survival of the fittest describes the same process and is accepted.

parts.workedSolution: Natural selection.

context.setting: Sorting five examples into natural selection and selective breeding

hints: For each one ask: did a person choose which ones bred, or did the environment decide who survived?
parts.stem:
Here are five examples.
A. A farmer breeds only from the hens that lay the most eggs.
B. Snails whose shells match the colour of the rocks are eaten less often by birds, so more of them breed.
C. A grower keeps seed only from the sweetest strawberry plants.
D. Rats that survive a poison leave more young, and many of their young survive it too.
E. Dog breeders mate the calmest dogs of each litter to produce calm guide dogs.
Choose the two letters that describe natural selection.

any: b
d

scheme.for: B
D
scheme.examinerNote: Either order. A third letter is a hedge and loses a mark, as the listing rule does.

parts.workedSolution: B and D: in both, the environment (birds, a poison) decides which ones survive to breed. In A, C and E a person chooses.

context.setting: Putting the stages of natural selection in order, for rats and a poison

hints: The variation has to be there before the poison does anything.
The change in the whole population is the result, so it comes last.
parts.stem: A farmer puts down a poison to control rats. After some years, most of the rats are not killed by it. The statements describe how this happened, but they are jumbled. Put them in the correct order, the first at the top.

items: The resistant rats survive and reproduce.
Over many generations, the proportion of resistant rats in the population increases.
Some rats in the population have a mutation that makes them resistant to the poison.
The resistant rats pass the resistance gene on to their offspring.
The poison kills most of the rats that are not resistant.

scheme.for: the mutation (variation) first
then the non-resistant killed, then the resistant survive and reproduce, then pass on the gene
the rise in the proportion of resistant rats last

parts.workedSolution: Some rats in the population have a mutation that makes them resistant to the poison. The poison kills most of the rats that are not resistant. The resistant rats survive and reproduce. The resistant rats pass the resistance gene on to their offspring. Over many generations, the proportion of resistant rats in the population increases.

scheme.examinerNote: Five creditworthy points for four marks, as on the Summer 2024 scheme: the mutation; the non-resistant dying; the resistant surviving; reproducing; passing on the gene. Any four earn full marks. Immunity or antibodies earn nothing.

parts.workedSolution: Some bacteria had a mutation that made them resistant. The antibiotic killed the bacteria that were not resistant. context.setting: Which explanation of a resistant population is right

hints: Which statement has the variation existing before the poison?
parts.stem: After years of the same poison being used, most rats in a city are resistant to it. Which statement correctly explains why?

options.text: Some rats were already resistant, and the poison killed most of the others.
options.feedback: That is natural selection: the variation was there first, and the poison removed the rats without resistance.

options.text: The rats changed their bodies so that the poison could not harm them.
options.feedback: No rat changes itself to survive. The resistant rats had the gene before the poison was ever used; the poison only removed the others.

options.text: The rats made antibodies against the poison.
options.feedback: This is not immunity, and antibodies are not involved. The Summer 2024 report found this confusion in answers about a poison-resistant population.

options.text: The poison made every rat mutate into a resistant rat.
options.feedback: The poison does not cause the mutation. Mutations are random and were already present in a few rats; the poison decides which rats survive.

scheme.for: some were already resistant; the poison killed most of the others

parts.workedSolution: Some rats were already resistant, and the poison killed most of the others.

parts.workedSolution: Birds with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds, so they survived. They reproduced and passed on the genes for deep beaks to their offspring, so over many generations the curve moves to deeper beaks.

context.setting: Resistant bacteria in a hospital's samples, ten years apart

hints: The resistant samples go on top; all the samples go on the bottom.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides all the samples by the resistant ones, so the fraction is upside down. A part of the samples cannot be more than 100% of them.
That is the percentage that were not resistant. The question asks about the resistant samples.

parts.stem: A hospital tested 400 samples of one type of bacterium in 2025. 140 of them were resistant to an antibiotic. Calculate the percentage of samples that were resistant.

hints: What does the antibiotic do to each kind of bacterium, and what do the survivors do next?

commonErrors.feedback: Resistance in a population is not immunity: no antibodies are involved. Tell it as selection instead: some already had the gene, the others died, the survivors reproduced and passed the gene on. The Summer 2024 report found answers drifting into immunity instead.

parts.stem: In 2015 the figure was 8%. The antibiotic was used a great deal in between. Suggest how using the antibiotic caused the percentage of resistant bacteria to rise.

accepted: the antibiotic killed the bacteria that were not resistant, so the resistant bacteria survived, reproduced and passed on the gene for resistance

commonErrors.feedback: Resistance in a population is not immunity: no antibodies are involved. Tell it as selection instead: some already had the gene, the others died, the survivors reproduced and passed the gene on. The Summer 2024 report found answers drifting into immunity instead.

Surviving is only half the chain. The next generation changes only because the survivors reproduce and pass on the gene for the useful characteristic. Finish with that link: the Summer 2024 report found answers that left it out.

parts.stem:
A crop plant makes a poison in its leaves that kills beetles that eat them. In one area a few beetles could eat the leaves without harm. Over several years, most of the beetles in the area became able to eat the leaves.
Use the information and what you know about natural selection to explain how this happened.

accepted: some beetles had a mutation that made them resistant to the poison; the beetles that were not resistant were poisoned and died; the resistant beetles survived and reproduced; they passed the resistance gene on to their offspring

context.setting: From variation to new species, or to extinction

hints: Start with variation and end with extinction.
One link a sentence: variation, competition, survival, inheritance, many generations, new species, extinction.

commonErrors.feedback: Resistance in a population is not immunity: no antibodies are involved. Tell it as selection instead: some already had the gene, the others died, the survivors reproduced and passed the gene on. The Summer 2024 report found answers drifting into immunity instead.

parts.stem:
Explain how natural selection can lead to the evolution of a new species, and why a species that fails to adapt to a change in its environment may become extinct.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: there is variation in a population, from mutations and sexual reproduction
there is competition for resources, so not all individuals survive
the best adapted individuals are more likely to survive
the survivors reproduce and pass on their genes
this continues over many generations, causing gradual change: evolution
populations can change so much that a new species forms
if the environment changes and no individuals are adapted to it, none survive to reproduce and the species becomes extinct

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: The Summer 2024 report calls natural selection a topic candidates find difficult, and records answers that drifted from passing on the advantageous gene into immunity. An answer that never says the survivors reproduce and pass on their genes has lost the link that makes the chain work, and should not reach the top band. Evolution forming a new species is Higher Tier content.

parts.workedSolution: In any population there is variation, caused by mutations and sexual reproduction. More young are produced than the resources can support, so there is competition and not all survive: the best adapted are more likely to survive. The survivors reproduce and pass on their genes, so their characteristics become more common in the next generation. This continues over many generations, causing gradual change, which is evolution. Two populations living in different conditions can change so much that a new species forms. But if the environment changes and no individuals are adapted to the new conditions, none survive to reproduce, and the species becomes extinct.

findTheMistake.stem: Cara explains how the rats in a city became resistant to a poison, one mark a line. Her answer:
studentWorking: Some rats had a mutation that made them resistant to the poison.
The rats made antibodies against the poison, so they became immune.
The resistant rats survived and reproduced.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 turns natural selection into immunity. The rats without the mutation were killed by the poison; the resistant ones made no antibodies, they were resistant already.
correction: Some rats had a mutation that made them resistant to the poison.
The poison killed the rats that were not resistant.
The resistant rats survived and reproduced.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand. The Summer 2024 report found exactly this drift: detailed writing about immunity and antibodies where the mark needed the selection chain.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh describes a dish of bacteria before and after an antibiotic is added. Her answer:
studentWorking: Before the antibiotic, all the bacteria divide and a few become resistant by mutation.
After the antibiotic, the original bacteria and the resistant bacteria both keep dividing.
So the dish ends up with more bacteria than before.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 leaves the original bacteria alive. The antibiotic kills them; only the resistant bacteria are left to divide.
correction: Before the antibiotic, all the bacteria divide and a few become resistant by mutation.
After the antibiotic, only the resistant bacteria keep dividing.
So the dish ends up with resistant bacteria only.
findTheMistake.feedback: The Summer 2025 report found many candidates drawing original bacteria that had survived the antibiotic. After it, only the resistant kind is in the dish.

findTheMistake.stem: A question shows four tomato plants: A tall with many small fruits, B tall with a few small fruits, C tall with a few large fruits, D short with a few small fruits. It asks which two to breed for short plants with large fruits, and why. Eoin's answer:
studentWorking: Because they are the best plants.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 names nothing. The explanation mark is for what each plant brings: C has the large fruits and D is short.
correction: Because C has large fruits and D is short.
findTheMistake.feedback: The letters earn their mark. The Summer 2023 report found the right letters followed by careless explanations, which lost the second.

findTheMistake.stem: Beetles became resistant to a crop plant's poison. Then some crop plants began to make a stronger poison. A question asks for the advantage to the crop plants. Oisín's answer:
studentWorking: The stronger poison is the plants' advantage.
More of the beetles are killed, so the beetle population falls.
So fewer beetles are left to eat the crop.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 answers about the beetles. The question asks what the plants gain: fewer of them are eaten, so more of them survive to reproduce.
correction: The stronger poison is the plants' advantage.
Fewer of the crop plants are eaten, so more of them survive to reproduce.
So fewer beetles are left to eat the crop.
findTheMistake.feedback: The Summer 2024 report: too many candidates gave the effect on the other species and lost this mark. Write about the population the question names.

prompts.prompt: Give the four steps of natural selection, in order.
prompts.answer: Variation; not all survive; the best adapted survive and reproduce; they pass on their genes.

prompts.prompt: Does an antibiotic make bacteria resistant?
prompts.answer: No. Some were already resistant through a mutation; the antibiotic killed the rest.

prompts.prompt: What is left in a dish of bacteria a day after an antibiotic is added?
prompts.answer: Only resistant bacteria, and more of them, because they divide.
A continuing process of natural selection causing gradual change over time; it may form a new species.

prompts.prompt: Why can a species become extinct when its environment changes?
prompts.answer: It fails to adapt: no individual suits the new conditions, so they all die before they can reproduce.
Humans choose individuals with a desirable characteristic and breed them, over many generations, until all the offspring show it.

prompts.prompt: Name three kinds of characteristic that breeders select for.
prompts.answer: Appearance, more or better food, and disease resistance.

prompts.prompt: What is the one difference between natural selection and selective breeding?
prompts.answer: Who chooses: the environment in natural selection, humans in selective breeding.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for the advantage to one population. What must your answer be about?
prompts.answer: That population itself: what the change does for it, not for the other species.

prompts.prompt: After the environment changes, where does the peak of a population's curve move?
prompts.answer: Towards the value that now suits the environment best, over many generations.
